title: Beyond the Gallery Talk: How The Met Invites Artists to Think Out Loud
content:
What happens when you ask an artist not to explain a work of art, but to have a conversation with it?

At the Creative Museums Summit 2026, Isaac Poole, Associate Educator in Public Programs at The Metropolitan Museum of Art shared an exciting programme that set out to explore this question.

Most museum talks are built on interpretation: an expert stands before an object and tells us what it means. The Met’s Explorations series turns that around. Artists, playwrights, designers and choreographers are invited into direct dialogue with objects in the collection, responding through the methods of their own discipline. The focus is on their personal relationship with a work, not commentary about it.

The results have ranged from an audio guide that becomes a meditation, to a dance performed before a Tiffany window, to a comedy in which a marble muse talks back. Together they offer a model for reaching adult audiences that any museum can learn from.
snippet: What happens when you ask an artist not to explain a work of art, but to have a conversation with it?
creator: Manuel Charr

title: How National Museums Liverpool Built an Adult Craft Programme That Pays Its Way
content:
Faced with flat budgets and a new target to generate income, National Museums Liverpool’s Learning and Participation team launched a £20 hands-on craft series for adults. Two years on, Meet and Make is paying its way, funding free community sessions and helping strangers become friends. Participation facilitator Faye Richardson-Hignett shared how it works at the Creative Museums Summit.

Most adults stop making art somewhere around the end of school. Somewhere along the way, many decide they are “not creative” and quietly opt out.

Meet and Make was designed to undo that. Each month, National Museums Liverpool (NML) runs a two-hour workshop where adults try a craft, perhaps for the first time in years. The brief to participants is simple: drop any expectation that the result has to be good, have a go, then head to the café for a brew and a chat.

“The whole aim of this is to make it really, really simple, really, really easy,” Richardson-Hignett told the Summit. Her hope is that other museums will see how achievable it is and try something similar.
